item.title: Edgar Snow's pursuit of truth resonates in a divided world, 90 years on
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
by Xinhua writers Yang Shilong, Liu Yanan NEW YORK, Nov. 22 (Xinhua) -- Nearly 90 years ago, American journalist Edgar Snow challenged the assumptions surrounding China's little-known Communist movement with a simple question: "How did they know? They had never been to Red China." Rather than relying on secondhand accounts, Snow broke through layers of blockade and traveled into northwestern China in 1936 to find out for himself. His reporting led to Red Star Over China, a landmark book that introduced the movement and its leaders to a wide international audience. Nine decades later, Snow's question remains relevant: How much do people really know about other countries, and how much do they simply assume? At a symposium held in New York early this month, American and Chinese scholars and representatives of organizations preserving Snow's legacy reflected on the continuing importance of independent, fact-based journalism in a world marked by growing mistrust and competing political narratives. The event was jointly hosted by Xinhua News Agency, Peking University and the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation, focusing on the contemporary value and global significance of Snow's spiritual legacy. "Everyone has in their mind a picture of another country," said Brad Kleindl, co-president of the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation. Snow and his companion, Helen Foster Snow, helped shape the world's understanding of China at a crucial moment in its history, he said, adding that younger Americans today need more opportunities to learn about China and the history of relations between the two countries. Zhang Hong, professor at Beijing Institute of Technology, said Snow's achievements were rooted in years of reading, travel and engagement with ordinary people before his 1936 journey. "The power of communication ultimately depends on the depth of understanding," she said. Snow's handwritten interview questions, preserved among his papers -- part of the Edgar Snow Collection at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, illustrate that approach. Preparing to interview Mao Zedong, he asked about land reform, private property, foreign investment and China's relations with the outside world. He wanted to understand not only what the Communists believed, but how their ideas would work in practice. Snow also sought to distinguish his reporting from his personal political sympathies. "Wherever my personal sympathies may lie, I continue to be from Missouri," he wrote in a February 1937 letter to Nelson T. Johnson, the then U.S. ambassador to China. Missouri, known as the "Show-Me State," is associated with a demand for evidence rather than unsupported assertions. John Phillips, vice president of the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation, drew a similar distinction between discovering facts and influencing how they are presented. "Journalism is about discovery of facts but not putting your thumb on the scale," he said. Nancy Hill, president emeritus of the foundation, emphasized the importance of firsthand experience and the limits of individual observation. "You have to go to the place, know the people, know the culture, invest the time to fully understand the story," she said. Hill said each experience and observation provides only "one small biopsy," cautioning against drawing overly broad conclusions. Snow himself acknowledged errors in the original English edition of Red Star Over China in his 1938 preface to the Chinese edition, noting that some had been corrected. His work also reflected an awareness of journalism's lasting historical value. In the 1968 preface to a revised edition of Red Star Over China, Snow described the book as containing "not only a 'scoop' of perishable news but likewise of many facts of durable history." Chen Gang, dean of Peking University's School of Journalism and Communication, said Snow's reporting demonstrated the influence a journalist could have by investigating a political movement that was poorly understood abroad but would profoundly shape China's future. Chen called for training journalists with the historical perspective, social responsibility, independent judgment and practical skills that characterized Snow's work. The symposium also examined how new technologies could help preserve and study Snow's legacy. Wang Tianfu, a researcher at Peking University, proposed connecting digitized Snow archives held by institutions in different countries, allowing researchers to compare historical documents, photographs, interviews and accounts of the same events. He stressed that artificial intelligence could assist in such research but should not replace original historical evidence. Speakers also discussed efforts to introduce younger generations to the history of exchanges between China and the United States. Gao Minna, deputy director of China's Shaanxi Center for Edgar Snow Studies, pointed to youth exchange programs inspired by the work of Edgar and Helen Snow, including those bringing American students to China. She said the Helen Foster Snow Foundation has pledged to bring 5,000 American students to China and engage 30,000 students online over the next five years. Zhang, who first encountered Snow's archives while studying in Kansas in 2014, said the American journalist's legacy offered a continuing basis for exchanges between researchers and institutions in the two countries. "A bridge can connect two sides only when it has a solid foundation at both ends," she said. Zhang called for rigorous academic research and open international dialogue to carry forward Snow's legacy of crossing borders, understanding different societies and respecting facts. (Xinhua correspondents in New York Shi Chun, Xu Jing, videographer Vivien Liu also contributed to the report) ■

item.title: Exhibition highlights contributions of international friends in wartime China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
A man visits an exhibition at the Museum of the Communist Party of China in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 23, 2026. The exhibition titled "Great Bridge Builders Edgar Snow and International Friends in Yan'an" was opened here on Monday. Featuring the individual stories and collective memories of 216 international friends, the exhibition traces a historical journey from wartime support to enduring friendship. (Xinhua/Jin Liangkuai) BEIJING, Nov. 23 (Xinhua) -- An exhibition was launched in the Museum of the Communist Party of China (CPC) in Beijing on Monday highlighting the contributions of international friends, including American journalist Edgar Snow, during China's wartime years and paying tribute to friendships that transcended national borders. Titled "Great Bridge Builders: Edgar Snow and International Friends in Yan'an", the exhibition features 150 cultural relics and archival documents, 402 photographs, and seven documentaries. It tells the stories of international friends who broke through multiple blockades to reach Yan'an, China's revolutionary heartland, about 90 years ago, supported the Chinese revolution, and helped build a bridge of dialogue between the CPC, the Chinese people, and the world. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March by the Red Army under the leadership of the CPC, and also the 90th anniversary of Snow's first visit to the revolutionary base in northern Shaanxi, which inspired his renowned work "Red Star Over China." His works helped introduce the Chinese revolution in the 1930s to the world and inspired many other international people to visit Yan'an. The exhibition is co-hosted by the publicity department of the CPC Shaanxi provincial committee, the Museum of the CPC and the CPC Yan'an municipal committee, and organized by the Yan'an Revolutionary Memorial Hall. Highlights include a 1938 Chinese edition of Red Star Over China published in Shanghai, and an inscribed copy of Helen Snow's Inside Red China. Liu Ni, director of the Yan'an Revolutionary Memorial Hall, said that more items are being donated. For instance, Sharon Crain, a friend of Edgar Snow's wife Helen, donated two suitcases the couple once used. The suitcases are currently on the way to China. Visitors can also find items such as a camera used by American doctor George Hatem in Yan'an, a replica of German doctor Hans Muller's wallet, and documents from American experts Erwin Engst and Joan Hinton. "As descendants visiting this exhibition, viewing these artifacts and archival photos, we gain a deeper appreciation for the simple yet profound friendship our ancestors forged when they chose to put down roots in this land," said Dehua Muller, son of Hans. "We are committed to passing this friendship on." Fred Engst, son of Erwin Engst and Joan Hinton, observed that while official diplomacy serves as a "big bridge" between nations, people-to-people exchanges form the "small bridges." He explained: "The big bridge bears the critical mission of connecting countries, while the smaller bridges link the hearts of ordinary people. Only when both converge can mutual understanding truly endure." The exhibition will last for three months in Beijing. ■ A man visits an exhibition at the Museum of the Communist Party of China in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 23, 2026. item.title: China rolls out plan to improve eldercare, childcare services
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
BEIJING, Nov. 23 (Xinhua) -- China on Monday unveiled an action plan to improve services for the elderly and young children, as the country responds to an aging population and seeks to ease the burden of raising children. The plan, jointly issued by four government departments including the National Development and Reform Commission, sets a series of targets for 2030, including more accessible community-based eldercare services and a broader supply of affordable childcare. By 2030, the coverage rate of community-based eldercare institutions and facilities is expected to reach 70 percent. The enrollment rate of children under the age of three in childcare services is targeted to rise by 6 percentage points from its 2025 level. The plan aims to essentially establish a framework for inclusive eldercare and childcare services that are accessible in both urban and rural areas, reasonably distributed, affordable and of assured quality. The measures come as China faces growing demand for care services amid demographic changes. At the end of 2025, the country had 323.38 million people aged 60 and above, accounting for 23 percent of its total population, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. Experts believe the figures underscore the increasing need for accessible and professional eldercare services. To improve elderly care infrastructure, the plan vows to support building new facilities and upgrading existing ones. Particular attention will be given to 2,000 public elderly care institutions that are aging and in need of renovation, targeting improvements to the standard of care they provide and tightening their safety management measures. On childcare, the plan responds to widespread public concern about the difficulty of raising young children. It supports the conversion of eligible kindergartens to also serve children aged two to three, and calls for the development of nursery facilities within a 15-minute reach of residential areas -- the "15-minute childcare circle." In recent years, China has worked to encourage births and ease the strain on families. The government has extended maternity and paternity leave, introduced cash subsidies for newborns and simplified marriage registration. ■

item.title: China launches first actively managed ETFs amid capital market reform
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
BEIJING, Nov. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's first batch of actively managed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) began trading on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges on Monday, marking a new step in the country's efforts to deepen capital market reforms and attract long-term funds. Unlike traditional ETFs, which typically track an underlying benchmark, actively managed ETFs allow fund managers to select stocks and adjust portfolios in pursuit of returns that outperform a benchmark. Global active ETFs had reached 2.7 trillion U.S. dollars in assets under management as of the end of September 2026, accounting for 13 percent of the global ETF market, data showed. The sector has recorded net inflows for 78 consecutive months, reflecting growing demand for diversified wealth management products. The products combine the return potential of active management with the institutional advantages of ETFs, helping broaden equity investment options and channel more medium- and long-term capital into the market, said Jiao Caixia, an official with the China Securities Regulatory Commission. Market institutions said the launch would broaden China's range of ETF products, and provide insurers, pension funds and individual investors with relatively low-cost, convenient access to active investment strategies. China has stepped up efforts to deepen capital market reforms in recent years, including expanding the range of publicly offered equity funds and encouraging more long-term investment. As of the end of September 2026, 943 ETFs were listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange, with combined assets of 3.35 trillion yuan (about 499 billion U.S. dollars). Holdings by medium- and long-term investors totaled nearly 1.7 trillion yuan, accounting for more than half of the total, according to the exchange. ■

item.title: China leverages AI to accelerate power sector's intelligent transformation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
BEIJING, Nov. 23 (Xinhua) -- China is weaving artificial intelligence (AI) into the fabric of its power industry, reshaping the sector's entire operational workflow to advance its intelligent transformation. The efforts, revamping operations across generation, transmission, distribution and retail, seek to make power generation more controllable, create smarter grids, and ensure more precise supply-demand matching, according to industry insiders. BOOSTING POWER GENERATION EFFICIENCY In July, Yalong River Hydropower Development Company, Ltd. launched China's first AI-powered intelligent operating model for its 10-gigawatt integrated hydropower, wind and solar base in Sichuan Province, one of China's flagship integrated clean-energy complexes, with its total installed clean energy capacity slated to reach 78 gigawatts by 2035. The platform handles forecasting, dispatch, operational monitoring and market trading across the combined renewable portfolio, marking a breakthrough for AI deployment at large-scale clean energy hubs. Electricity is hard to store at large scale, requiring continuous real-time balancing between supply and demand. AI is addressing this longstanding operational challenge, delivering tighter control over generation, smarter grid scheduling and more accurate alignment of power supply and consumption. Within power generation, AI models deliver precise forecasts of wind, solar and hydrological resources, lifting the utilization rate of variable green power. "Previously, inflow analysis and operation planning involved meteorological data collection, data processing, forecast revision and plan validation," said Duan Tong, director of the hydrological information office at the company's central control center. The large AI model cuts this workflow from one to two hours to roughly 10 minutes, while raising inflow forecast accuracy by around 5 percent, said Duan. EXPANDING INTELLIGENT POWER DELIVERY AI is also transforming grid operations through virtual power plants, an emerging kind of digital coordination platform that pools flexible distributed load resources to deliver demand response. Powered by AI algorithms, these virtual assets allow the grid to absorb rising volumes of distributed energy resources and open grid-balancing participation to even everyday power consumers. At Chengdu's Shiyang charging station, electric vehicles can feed electricity back to the grid. Liu Chang, a supervisor with State Grid Sichuan's EV service arm, said vehicle owners received payments of 2 yuan (about 0.3 U.S. dollars) per kWh or 3 yuan for grid injections during peak hours amid this summer's heavy power demand. Once these distributed resources are connected to the virtual power plants, AI will optimize the charging and discharging schedule under conditions such as the range and battery level set by users, Liu said. China's virtual power plants hit a maximum adjustable capacity of 20.428 gigawatts at the end of June 2026, according to the National Energy Administration. Industry analysts expect AI to eventually tie generation forecasting, load forecasting and equipment fault detection into one unified coordination framework, connecting power plants, grids, energy storage assets and end users. The central government's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for the new-type power system backs this approach. It calls for unlocking power-sector data, building an AI-powered new power system, and rolling out digital and intelligent upgrades across the full electricity supply chain. An action plan released in April by the central authorities also sets targets for broadening AI adoption throughout the energy sector while expanding clean energy supplies to support AI computing loads by 2030. ■

item.title: China's sector-specific plans map out path to high-quality development
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-23
BEIJING, Nov. 23 (Xinhua) -- China has rolled out a series of sector-specific plans to translate its broader development vision into concrete action during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), providing detailed roadmaps for key areas of economic and social development. Covering fields ranging from manufacturing and energy to employment, education and health care, the plans set out specific targets, priority tasks and policy measures. Together, they offer a more detailed look at how the world's second-largest economy seeks to cultivate new growth drivers, address emerging development challenges and improve people's livelihoods as it pursues high-quality development amid global uncertainties. FROM BLUEPRINT TO ACTION Five-year plans have long played an important role in China's governance, providing strategic direction and policy continuity for the country's development. The overarching outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan, approved in March this year, sets out the country's overall development objectives through 2030. Sector-specific plans complement this general framework by breaking down national priorities into detailed targets, major projects and implementation arrangements for individual fields. Zhang Linshan, a researcher at the Academy of Macroeconomic Research under the National Development and Reform Commission, said sector-specific plans provide an important basis for guiding development in particular fields, allocating public resources, directing private investment and formulating relevant policies. Several of the recently released plans have established measurable targets for 2030. China's dedicated consumption plan aims to raise total retail sales of consumer goods to around 60 trillion yuan (8.94 trillion U.S. dollars), while the plan for building a new-type power system targets a 50-percent share for non-fossil energy in electricity generation. Other targets include raising average life expectancy to 80 years and reducing carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP by 17 percent from the 2025 level, reflecting a focus on both economic development and improvements in people's well-being. BREAKING NEW GROUND A notable feature of the latest round of sector-specific plans is that they cover certain fields for the first time, reflecting China's efforts to address emerging development challenges and respond to changing economic and social needs. Among them is the country's first national-level urban renewal plan, released in May, which calls for the construction and renovation of approximately 770,000 km of urban underground pipelines. The plan also calls for better use of existing land and stronger building safety management, reflecting a shift toward upgrading existing urban areas and improving the quality of urban life. Consumption expansion, disease prevention and control, and cultural heritage protection are among other fields covered by national-level sector-specific plans for the first time. The latest round also includes the first national-level plans dedicated to building China's strengths in finance, sports and tourism. Tian Xuan, dean of Peking University's Guanghua School of Management, said the new plans cover areas crucial to China's economic and social development over the next five years. Their introduction would further improve the country's planning system and help ensure the effective implementation of national development priorities, Tian said. HIGH-QUALITY DEVELOPMENT Beyond their expanding scope, the sector-specific plans share a central objective: advancing high-quality development by strengthening the real economy, fostering innovation and improving people's well-being. A plan to improve industrial foundational capabilities calls for stronger innovation platforms and measures to address weaknesses in key technologies. Another aims to consolidate China's competitive advantages in intelligent connected new energy vehicles and help the country join the ranks of global automotive powerhouses by 2030. Technological innovation is a recurring priority across several sector-specific plans, with measures to promote artificial intelligence applications, breakthroughs in all-solid-state battery technologies and research into frontier technologies. Green transition also features prominently, with plans calling for greener industrial development and closer coordination between electricity supply and computing power. Xin Yongfei, an expert at the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, said the sector-specific plans coordinate efforts in basic research, technological breakthroughs, commercialization and talent development to build momentum for high-quality development. The pursuit of high-quality development extends beyond industrial upgrading to improving people's livelihoods. The plan for implementing the employment-first strategy calls for promoting employment and entrepreneurship in response to advances in artificial intelligence and expanding job opportunities in services and emerging industries. Other plans seek to improve public services, including expanding enrollment capacity at general senior high schools, developing elderly-friendly communities and expanding access to affordable elderly care services. The plans are also meant to deliver benefits well beyond China's borders, with measures to expand imports of quality foreign products and deepen international cooperation. Koh King Kee, president of the Center for New Inclusive Asia, a Malaysian think tank, said China's sector-specific plans emphasize the development of new quality productive forces and signal a commitment to high-standard opening up and mutually beneficial cooperation. By turning more Chinese demand into development opportunities, the plans will continue to inject much-needed certainty into the global economy, Koh said. ■

item.title: Xi's speech marking 160th anniversary of Sun Yat-sen's birth published
item.description:

BEIJING, Nov. 23 (Xinhua) -- A speech delivered by Chinese President Xi Jinping at a ceremony marking the 160th anniversary of Sun Yat-sen's birth has been published as a booklet. item.title: China's tech innovation engine powers a connected Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22
* China's push to unleash the potential of innovation and share technological dividends through open regional integration has resonated widely -- translating its innovation capacity into broader market opportunities and lending fresh momentum to economic growth and the building of an Asia-Pacific community. * Across the Asia-Pacific, China's technological innovations are finding applications in a growing range of industries and aspects of everyday life. * The release of the Shenzhen Initiative marked a milestone in the 30-year history of the APEC CEO Summit. It was a historic moment in Shenzhen, a city that has stood at the forefront of China's opening-up and has grown into a global innovation hub. BEIJING, Nov. 22 (Xinhua) -- As host of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China has placed openness, innovation and cooperation at the heart of its agenda as the three priority areas. Throughout this week's sessions, participants explored how the Asia-Pacific can navigate structural shifts and cultivate new engines of economic growth. China's push to unleash the potential of innovation and share technological dividends through open regional integration has resonated widely -- translating its innovation capacity into broader market opportunities and lending fresh momentum to economic growth and the building of an Asia-Pacific community. INNOVATION THAT BENEFITS ALL At an experimental durian orchard at Chiang Mai University in Thailand, agricultural lecturer Supakorn Wongsuk prepares a drone for takeoff. Having studied in China, he now applies the technology to explore more efficient methods of cultivating tropical fruits. Lifting smoothly into the air, the drone glides above rows of durian trees, releasing a fine mist of pesticide across their leaves and branches. "Using drones to spray pesticides can improve operational efficiency, reduce farmers' direct exposure to chemicals, and protect their health and safety," said Supakorn. He sees the Chinese innovations as offering benefits that extend well beyond farming efficiency. "For young people, drone operations can also create new job opportunities." Across the Asia-Pacific, China's technological innovations are finding applications in a growing range of industries and aspects of everyday life. The role of innovation also drew sharp focus at the APEC CEO Summit 2026 in Shenzhen. "Innovation is very important, and innovation cannot be done overnight. It requires strong education support and accumulated experience. This is where we think China can play a role," said Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry Chairman Anindya N. Bakrie. "China has an important role to play," said Julien Leclair-Dionne, associate director at the University of Ottawa's Professional Development Institute. "Particularly given its technological capabilities, innovation ecosystem and experience in scaling emerging technologies." "Ultimately, what matters most is not simply how advanced the technologies become, but how effectively the innovations are translated into opportunities for people, organizations and communities across the region," he said. OPENNESS CREATES OPPORTUNITIES Released on Wednesday, the Shenzhen Initiative of the APEC CEO Summit 2026 highlighted the transformative potential of frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence, while recognizing the accompanying risks and regulatory challenges that require coordinated regional oversight. At the heart of the document lies a clear, unified conviction among business leaders: no single economy can capture the promise of breakthrough technology -- or tame its disruptions -- alone; only deep regional cooperation can turn innovation into shared prosperity. Auckland Business Chamber CEO Simon Bridges emphasized the need for cooperation amid global uncertainty. "I think cooperation is probably the byword of APEC. And we know in the world right now, it's more important than ever," he said. China's approach to AI development provides "a very good example" that allows others to learn from its technological advances, he added. The appeal of Chinese AI models has become increasingly evident across the region. In South Korea, nearly half of the AI models released by local developers on Hugging Face, a globally popular open-source platform, between January and August this year were based on Chinese foundation models. "China has adopted AI with more open-weight, open-source, low-cost models that are going to be used by businesses around the world," said Jacob Cooke, CEO of WPIC Marketing + Technologies, a leading e-commerce and technology consultancy. "These Chinese companies have done their best to get this technology out to help people," Cooke said at the summit. The release of the Shenzhen Initiative marked a milestone in the 30-year history of the APEC CEO Summit. It was a historic moment in Shenzhen, a city that has stood at the forefront of China's opening-up and has grown into a global innovation hub. For Lee Ju-kwan, director of the National Center for APEC Studies at the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy of South Korea, Shenzhen's relentless innovation engine came vividly into focus during a visit to electric vehicle giant BYD's headquarters, offering a firsthand look at the homegrown tech muscle powering the city. "I was deeply impressed by what I saw, particularly robots performing tasks that would traditionally be carried out by human workers on the production line," Lee said. "This year, by hosting APEC, China has taken the opportunity to put forward and renew initiatives aimed at promoting openness and cooperation. I believe these efforts deserve attention and support," Lee said. GREEN INNOVATION "It's the most fantastic ride," said Jeffrey Sachs, a professor at Columbia University, looking back on an epic 15,000-km summer odyssey from Rome to China's Hong Kong, retracing Marco Polo's historic path behind the wheel of a BYD electric vehicle. Sachs said the journey showed how far green technology had advanced. "The technology is already here. Most of it is in its most advanced stage in China," Sachs said during a high-level panel at the APEC CEO Summit 2026. He also noted that China had significantly reduced the cost of green technologies, making the transition more affordable. "To go green is not to make an extra burden for the sake of the planet. It's just to have a low-cost, resilient, state-of-the-art energy system," he said. The benefits of China's green innovation are also being felt by residents of Goulburn in New South Wales, Australia. With an integrated solar-and-storage solution supplied by a Chinese company, the local community has brought its own solar farm into operation. The facility began supplying electricity to the grid in March, with part of its annual profits to be channeled into a community fund to help residents facing energy poverty. "For a long time, it has been talk around the kitchen table. Suddenly here we are in amongst the panels, watching the sun send electrons to the people and my kids all own little parts of this with the community," said Goulburn resident Dave Suttle. "Without China's involvement, we definitely wouldn't have solar cells as cheap as now," Martin Green, Scientia Professor of Photovoltaic and Renewable Energy Engineering at the University of New South Wales, told Xinhua. Having worked with China's photovoltaic industry for more than four decades, Green is now collaborating with Chinese partners on the next generation of solar technology. "Working with China, we feel we're in a position to improve the solar performance more quickly," he said. ■
